cur:catacombs-ponziano-bust-of-christ.summary: Christ appears as a frontal bust with a cross-nimbus, large eyes, short beard and long hair, set within an arched frame above a painted inscription. The austere, hieratic face belongs to the age of icons and shows how the catacombs continued to be decorated for pilgrims long after burials there had ceased.
facts: Commons dates the painting to about the 6th–7th century, from Wilpert's 1903 plate.
The Catacomb of Pontian, on the Via Portuense, is also known for a painted baptistery and frescoes of the martyrs Abdon and Sennen.
Painting reproduced from Joseph Wilpert, Die Malereien der Katakomben Roms (Freiburg, 1903), whose plates were photographed in the catacombs and hand-coloured in front of the originals.

cur:manuscripts-ramsey-psalter-crucifixi.summary: In delicate tinted line drawing, Christ hangs dead on the cross, his head sunk on his shoulder, beneath the inscription 'Hic est Nazarenus rex Iudeorum'; the Virgin, at left, raises her veil to her weeping face, and John, at right, writes on a scroll while gazing up at him. The fluttering drapery and fine, nervous line make this one of the most moving images in Anglo-Saxon art.
facts: Wikipedia notes that this coloured outline drawing draws on the style of the Utrecht Psalter, which was then in England.
The same artist seems to have worked at Fleury Abbey and at Saint-Bertin, Saint-Omer, where he contributed to the Boulogne Gospels.
The psalter's script inspired the 'foundational hand' of the 20th-century calligrapher Edward Johnston.

cur:monumental-naples-baptistery-peter-o.summary: A haloed, beardless Christ in white stands at the left, turned towards a blue sea full of fish, where a figure in the water reaches towards him; above, a man sits in a boat. The incomplete scene has been read as the Miraculous Draught of Fishes, as Christ saving Peter from the waves, or as the calling of Peter and Andrew.
facts: Of the scenes once set within garlands around the dome, four survive: the Traditio Legis, the Samaritan woman with the Wedding at Cana, the Miraculous Draught (or Peter on the water), and the women at the tomb.

The baptistery of San Giovanni in Fonte beside Naples Cathedral is one of the oldest in the West; its building is dated to the 4th century, and its construction is attributed to Bishop Severus (362–408) or to later bishops.

cur:monumental-naples-baptistery-peter-o.notes: The exact Gospel episode is uncertain; scholars propose the Miraculous Draught, Peter walking on the water, a combination of both, or the calling of Peter and Andrew.

Q87665248.summary: Under a pierced arch the central panel shows the Nativity: the Virgin reclines beside the manger where the swaddled Christ Child lies with the ox and ass, angels crowd above, and in the foreground the newborn is bathed. The wings continue the story of Christ's victory in small, crowded scenes, among them the Entry into Jerusalem, the Descent into Limbo and the Ascension. A portable triptych like this gathered the great feasts into a single object for private prayer.
facts: Greek inscriptions name the scenes: the Nativity at the centre, the Entry into Jerusalem and the Descent into Limbo on the left wing, and the Ascension on the right.
The Louvre dates the triptych to 950–1000 on stylistic grounds and places it in Constantinople under the Macedonian dynasty.
It passed through the collections of Prince Alexis Soltykoff (sold 1861), Frédéric Spitzer and Edmond Foulc before the Louvre bought it from Raoul Duseigneur in 1900.
Q87665248.notes: Original title: Triptyque : la Nativité (OA 5004). The Louvre's date text reads '2e moitié du Xe siècle'.
